Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Maria had always been a force to be reckoned with in her professional life. As a project manager, she was known for her sharp mind and quick thinking. But it all changed when she was held captive by a group of armed men during a business trip to South America. The memory of being locked in a small room, unable to escape or call for help, still haunted her. Even now, years after the event, Maria found herself avoiding confined spaces whenever possible. Elevators made her anxious, and she would often take the stairs instead. Her neck pain, which had started during her captivity, was a constant reminder of those terrifying days. She couldn't shake off the feeling that she was trapped, even when she knew it wasn't rational. As she navigated her daily routine, Maria felt like she was constantly on edge. She would catch herself checking the locks at home multiple times, making sure she was safe inside. The feeling of being "on guard" had become so ingrained that she couldn't relax, even in her own living room. Her family and friends noticed the change in her, but Maria struggled to explain it. She just knew that she felt like danger was lurking around every corner. Maria's fears had become all-consuming. She couldn't shake off the thought that you never know who will harm you. It was a constant refrain in her mind, making her feel like she was walking on eggshells. This fear had seeped into other areas of her life as well. She felt emotionally numb, like she was just going through the motions. Her usual optimism and joy were gone, replaced by a deep-seated sadness. As Maria tried to make sense of her emotions, she found herself ruminating on what she could have done differently during her captivity. If only she had been more careful, if only she had fought back harder... The self-blame was suffocating, and it led her down a rabbit hole of overanalysing every detail of the event. She would replay conversations with her captors, wondering if there was something she could have said or done to change the outcome. But Maria's attempts to regain control through magical thinking only made things worse. When she told herself that the event wasn't that bad or didn't really happen, it felt like a temporary reprieve, but ultimately, it just delayed the inevitable crash back into reality. Her mind would spin with worst-case scenarios, making her feel even more trapped and helpless. As the days turned into weeks, Maria's maladaptive strategies began to take their toll. She became withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and events that might trigger another panic attack. Her work suffered as well; she found herself second-guessing every decision, afraid of making a mistake that would put her in harm's way again. Despite her best efforts, Maria couldn't shake off the feeling of being trapped. It was like she was stuck in a never-ending cycle of fear and self-doubt. She knew she needed help to break free from this prison of her own mind. That's when she finally decided to seek therapy, hoping that someone could help her find a way out of the darkness that had consumed her life. As Maria sat in the therapist's office, she felt a glimmer of hope for the first time in years. Maybe, just maybe, she could learn to escape the trauma that had held her captive for so long and rediscover the happy person she used to be.
